strengths: Proposes a clear and intuitive extension of locate-then-edit methods by constraining both the key and residual/value-side update to smaller subspaces, addressing an important failure mode: unintended perturbation of unrelated knowledge.
Empirical results are broad for this subarea, covering LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, and Qwen2.5-7B on CounterFact and zsRE, with comparisons to strong baselines including MEMIT, PMET, and AlphaEdit.

Reported gains in specificity are substantial, especially on CounterFact, while efficacy remains high; additional 5,000-edit, CHED, general-capability, ablation, and hyperparameter analyses strengthen the empirical story.

The ablations show that the key-subspace and residual-subspace components have complementary effects, and the paper makes a reasonable effort to connect the method to perturbation analyses at entity last-token positions.
weaknesses: The central subspace interpretation is not fully convincing. Top-SVD directions over subject keys are assumed to be entity-agnostic, but the validation is indirect and partly circular; variance comparisons and update-proportion measurements do not establish that these subspaces encode the claimed semantic factors.

The residual-side method is technically under-justified. The two-direction swap assumption, orthogonality approximation, and learned directions w1/w2 are motivated heuristically, and the analysis itself shows the directions are not disentangled as hypothesized.

Evaluation choices may inflate the apparent gains. CounterFact evaluation is restricted to examples where the model already predicts the old object for rewrite, paraphrase, and neighborhood prompts, and specificity is measured via old-vs-new object comparisons rather than broader behavioral preservation.

Baseline reproducibility and fairness are not fully clear. The paper relies on EasyEdit/default hyperparameters for several methods, MEND/ROME results appear extremely poor in places, and there is limited discussion of whether baselines were carefully tuned under the same sequential-edit setting.

No uncertainty estimates, significance tests, or runtime/memory comparisons are provided, despite the method requiring SVD-based subspace construction and per-edit optimization of directions. This makes it hard to assess robustness and practical cost.
Reproducibility is limited because code and data are only promised after publication, and several implementation details that may affect performance are relegated to brief appendix descriptions.

The writing and presentation have noticeable polish issues, table formatting problems, and some imprecise claims such as saying the results confirm successful identification of critical subspaces when the evidence mainly supports improved empirical performance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and active problem: factual knowledge editing in LLMs with high specificity after sequential edits.

The proposed idea of constraining both the key and residual/value updates to subspaces is intuitive and potentially useful, especially as an extension of locate-then-edit methods such as MEMIT and AlphaEdit.
The evaluation covers multiple model families, including LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, and Qwen2.5-7B, and compares against several relevant editing baselines.
The reported gains in specificity on CounterFact are large, and the paper includes ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, and some analyses of perturbation/subspace behavior.
weaknesses: The technical justification is weak. The central claims about entity-specific and entity-agnostic subspaces are mostly asserted from the Linear Representation Hypothesis, but the actual SVD procedure does not convincingly establish that top singular directions correspond to entity-agnostic features. The variance analysis is too indirect to validate the semantic interpretation.

The residual-vector method is under-motivated and mathematically fragile. The claim that a two-dimensional subspace spanned by w1 and w2 captures the critical object-editing directions is not well justified, and the additive 'swap' derivation relies on an orthogonality assumption that is only encouraged by a penalty, not guaranteed.

The experimental evidence is not sufficient to support the strength of the claims. The main improvements are concentrated on standard editing benchmarks whose metrics are known to be narrow, and the paper does not convincingly test broader factual consistency, multi-hop effects, open-ended generation, adversarial paraphrases, or realistic temporal update scenarios.

The evaluation protocol raises concerns. Filtering CounterFact to cases where the model already predicts the old object on rewrite, paraphrase, and neighborhood prompts may substantially change the difficulty and comparability of results. The paper does not provide enough detail on how many examples remain, variance across runs, or statistical significance.

The comparison to baselines may not be fully fair or transparent. Hyperparameters are mostly inherited from prior work or EasyEdit, while SUIT has method-specific settings fixed without a clear validation protocol. Some baseline numbers are extremely poor, e.g. MEND and ROME in several settings, which makes the implementation and tuning questionable.

The general capability evaluation is weak. Reporting average F1 across a small set of GLUE/MMLU-style tasks after edits is useful, but the results are noisy and sometimes odd, with very low pre-edit scores for some models/tasks. This undermines confidence that the GC conclusions reflect real preservation of model ability.

The analysis sections often overclaim. Lower perturbation at subject last-token positions and smaller interaction with the constructed common subspace do not necessarily imply better preservation of unrelated knowledge or successful localization of factual features.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper says code and data will be released upon publication, but does not provide enough implementation detail for the optimization of w1 and w2, data filtering, exact prompts, computational cost, or runtime overhead to make the method readily reproducible.

The writing contains several clarity and polish issues, including inconsistent notation, typos, awkward phrasing, and some unsupported causal language such as claiming the results 'confirm' the subspace hypothesis.

Overall, despite some promising empirical numbers, the paper does not provide the level of technical grounding, evaluation rigor, or reproducibility expected for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and technically plausible extension of locate-then-edit knowledge editing: constraining both the key and residual/value-side update to lower-dimensional subspaces. The method is well motivated by the linear representation hypothesis and integrates naturally with MEMIT/AlphaEdit-style closed-form updates.

Empirical results are strong on the main CounterFact setting across LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, and Qwen2.5-7B. The specificity improvements over AlphaEdit are especially compelling, while edit efficacy remains high.

The evaluation includes several useful dimensions beyond headline edit success: generation quality, general capability benchmarks, sequential 1,000-edit results, a 5,000-edit setting, CHED contextual robustness, probability-based metrics, and extended baselines in the appendix.

The analysis section is stronger than average for this area. The perturbation heatmaps, layerwise MLP-output distances, subspace variance analysis, hyperparameter sweeps, and component ablations all help substantiate why the method may preserve unrelated knowledge better than prior methods.
The method appears practical for modern 6B-8B open models and uses widely studied benchmarks and baselines, making the contribution relevant to current work on factual model editing.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: SUIT builds directly on MEMIT/AlphaEdit and mainly changes how the key and residual vectors are constrained. The paper would benefit from sharper positioning relative to prior null-space and representation-restricted editing methods.

Several core claims about identifying entity-specific and object-relevant subspaces are stronger than the evidence. For example, higher variance of projected key components does not by itself establish semantic entity-specificity, and the w1/w2 analysis is mostly correlational and based on steering behavior rather than a rigorous disentanglement test.

The evaluation is not uniformly dominant. On ZSRE, SUIT is slightly worse than AlphaEdit on GPT-J overall S and on Qwen overall S/generalization, so the broad claim of setting a new standard should be softened.

Important reproducibility details are limited. The code is only promised after publication, runtime and memory overhead are not reported, and the optimization procedure for w1/w2 would benefit from more detail about initialization, convergence, per-edit cost, and sensitivity across seeds.

The CounterFact filtering criterion evaluates only cases where the pre-edit model already predicts the old object for rewrite, paraphrase, and neighborhood prompts. This is defensible, but it may bias the benchmark toward a cleaner subset and makes direct comparability to some prior reported numbers less clear.

There are presentation and consistency issues. Some appendix/table numbers appear inconsistent with the main tables, such as general capability values in the extended CounterFact results, and there are minor typos and notation slips that should be cleaned up before publication.

The general capability evaluation is useful but narrow and somewhat noisy; the paper reports average F1 over heterogeneous tasks, but does not provide statistical uncertainty or enough discussion of why some tasks/models improve or degrade after editing.

strengths: Clear and relevant contribution: the paper proposes a subspace-aware variant of locate-then-edit model editing that modifies both the key representation and residual/value update, targeting an important weakness of existing editing methods: specificity under sequential edits.

Empirical results are strong on standard editing benchmarks. Across LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, and Qwen2.5-7B, SUIT substantially improves specificity and harmonic mean scores over MEMIT, PMET, and AlphaEdit while largely preserving efficacy.

The evaluation is broader than many model-editing papers: it includes multiple model families, COUNTERFACT and ZSRE, 1000-edit sequential settings, additional baselines in the appendix, CHED/contextual robustness, a 5000-edit stress setting, RippleEdits, and a 13B-scale experiment.

Ablations and analyses are useful. The paper separately evaluates the key-subspace and residual-subspace components, studies hyperparameter tradeoffs, and provides perturbation analyses that support the intuition that SUIT induces smaller changes at subject-token positions.
The method is relatively simple and compatible with existing closed-form update machinery, making the work potentially useful to researchers already using MEMIT/AlphaEdit-style editing pipelines.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claims are only partially supported. The interpretation of top singular directions as entity-agnostic and the complement as entity-specific is plausible but heuristic; variance and perturbation analyses do not conclusively establish that the identified subspaces correspond to the claimed semantic factors.

The residual-vector formulation relies on a strong two-dimensional swap assumption. The paper itself observes that the learned directions are not disentangled, with each direction affecting both old and new objects. This weakens the claimed mechanistic explanation, even if the empirical method works.

Evaluation choices reduce comparability and may inflate perceived robustness. COUNTERFACT is filtered to cases where the model already predicts the old object for rewrite, paraphrase, and neighborhood prompts, while ZSRE uses a different token-level partial-credit criterion and a preservation reference based on the model’s pre-edit output rather than gold answers.

The paper would benefit from stronger reproducibility evidence. Code/data are promised only upon publication; implementation details for optimization, compute cost of per-edit direction learning, and exact baseline tuning are not fully sufficient to rule out sensitivity to engineering choices.

The main benchmarks remain narrow factual association tests. The general capability evaluation is useful but shallow, and there is limited evidence about effects on instruction-following, open-ended QA, reasoning, calibration, safety-relevant behavior, or edits involving longer/compositional facts.

Some presentation issues and inconsistencies remain, such as typos, dense notation, table formatting problems, and apparent mismatches between text and table values. These do not invalidate the work but make the claims harder to audit.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: reducing unintended side effects in locate-then-edit knowledge editing, especially under sequential edits.

The proposed idea of constraining both key and residual/value updates to lower-dimensional subspaces is intuitive and potentially useful, and it is simple enough to integrate with existing MEMIT/AlphaEdit-style updates.
The empirical section covers multiple model families, including LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B, and an additional LLaMA2-13B experiment, with comparisons to several editing baselines.

The reported CounterFact results show large specificity improvements over AlphaEdit while maintaining high efficacy, and the appendices include additional ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, and some contextual/ripple-effect evaluations.
weaknesses: The main technical interpretation is weakly justified. The paper defines the entity-agnostic key subspace as the span of top singular vectors of uncentered subject key vectors, but high-energy principal directions across subjects do not necessarily correspond to features that activate similarly across entities. The claimed entity-specific/entity-agnostic decomposition is therefore not well established.

Several analyses are close to tautological or insufficiently diagnostic. For example, the higher variance of the residual component after removing top SVD directions does not convincingly prove semantic entity-specificity, and the low interaction with the removed subspace partly follows from the construction of the projected key update.

The residual-vector method is under-motivated. The two directions w1 and w2 are optimized mainly to increase the new-object probability, yet the paper interprets them as distinct new-object promotion and old-object suppression directions. The authors themselves show that these roles are not disentangled, weakening the central subspace story.

The ZSRE evaluation is problematic. Main-table specificity is redefined to preserve the model's own answer immediately before each edit batch rather than the dataset answer or the original pre-edit answer, making the metric lenient and not directly comparable to prior work. The stricter appendix numbers are much lower for LLaMA, which substantially tempers the main claim.

Baseline reliability is a concern. Some baselines have near-zero or surprisingly poor results, and the paper appears to rely heavily on default/EasyEdit hyperparameters where original settings are unavailable. This makes it hard to know whether the large gains reflect a genuinely stronger method or uneven baseline tuning/evaluation choices.

The paper reports no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds/runs, despite large claims and potentially high sensitivity to edit ordering, sample filtering, batch construction, and hyperparameter selection.

The experimental protocol filters CounterFact to cases where the model already predicts the old object on rewrite, paraphrase, and neighborhood prompts. This may be defensible, but it changes the evaluated distribution and should be analyzed more carefully, especially because specificity is central to the claims.

Reproducibility is limited: code and data are only promised after publication, implementation details for optimization and baseline tuning are incomplete, and computational cost for the per-edit residual-direction optimization is not clearly compared against baselines in end-to-end editing time.

Overall, the paper has an interesting direction and some promising empirical signals, but the central mechanistic claims are not convincingly supported and the evaluation choices, especially for ZSRE and baselines, leave too much uncertainty for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Clear and meaningful contribution: SUIT introduces a subspace-aware modification of locate-then-edit methods, constraining both the key vector and residual/value update in a way that is well motivated by linear representation hypotheses.

Strong empirical performance across several models and benchmarks. The reported gains in specificity over AlphaEdit, MEMIT, and PMET on COUNTERFACT are large, while efficacy and generalization remain competitive or best-in-class.

Evaluation is fairly broad for this subarea: three main models, two standard datasets, sequential editing, additional baselines in the appendix, probability-based and generation-based metrics, general capability checks, CHED contextual robustness, RippleEdits, and a 5,000-edit stress test.

The ablations and analyses are useful. The paper separately studies the key-subspace and residual-subspace components, sensitivity to hyperparameters, perturbation at entity last-token positions, and evidence that the learned directions capture much of the useful update signal.

The method is relatively simple to integrate into the existing MEMIT/AlphaEdit framework and the paper gives enough algorithmic and hyperparameter detail to make the approach understandable and likely reproducible once code is released.
weaknesses: The core conceptual novelty is moderate rather than transformative: the method is an elegant extension of existing locate-then-edit/null-space editing ideas, but much of the machinery and evaluation setup inherits directly from MEMIT and AlphaEdit.

Some of the representation claims are stronger than the evidence. Higher variance in one projected subspace and reduced update interaction with another are suggestive, but do not fully establish that the subspaces cleanly correspond to entity-specific versus entity-agnostic features.

The ZSRE specificity protocol is nonstandard and partly self-referential, using the model's own previous generations as preservation targets. The authors justify this, but it complicates comparison with prior work and makes some ZSRE gains harder to interpret.

The main analyses and ablations are mostly on LLaMA3-8B and COUNTERFACT, so it is less clear whether the mechanistic explanation and hyperparameter stability hold as strongly across all evaluated models and datasets.

Reproducibility is not yet complete because code and data are promised only upon publication. Given the many implementation-sensitive details in knowledge editing, immediate release or more exact procedural detail would strengthen confidence.

The method has a nontrivial precomputation stage for constructing subject subspaces, and although the appendix quantifies this cost, the practical tradeoff versus simpler editing methods could be discussed more directly.
